verses.text: They continued three years without war between Syria and Israel.
In the third year, Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel.
The king of Israel said to his servants, “You know that Ramoth Gilead is ours, and we do nothing, and don’t take it out of the hand of the king of Syria?”
He said to Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to battle to Ramoth Gilead?” Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.”
Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire first for Yahweh’s word.”

Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said to them, “Should I go against Ramoth Gilead to battle, or should I refrain?” They said, “Go up; for the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
But Jehoshaphat said, “Isn’t there here a prophet of Yahweh, that we may inquire of him?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of Yahweh, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.” Jehoshaphat said, “Don’t let the king say so.”
Then the king of Israel called an officer, and said, “Quickly get Micaiah the son of Imlah.”

Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting each on his throne, arrayed in their robes, in an open place at the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets were prophesying before them.
Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made himself horns of iron, and said, “Yahweh says, ‘With these you will push the Syrians, until they are consumed.’”
All the prophets prophesied so, saying, “Go up to Ramoth Gilead, and prosper; for Yahweh will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
The messenger who went to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, “See now, the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth. Please let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak good.”
Micaiah said, “As Yahweh lives, what Yahweh says to me, that I will speak.”

When he had come to the king, the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth Gilead to battle, or shall we forbear?” He answered him, “Go up and prosper; and Yahweh will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
The king said to him, “How many times do I have to adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in Yahweh’s name?”
He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?”
Micaiah said, “Therefore hear Yahweh’s word. I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.
Yahweh said, ‘Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?’ One said one thing; and another said another.
A spirit came out and stood before Yahweh, and said, ‘I will entice him.’
Yahweh said to him, ‘How?’ He said, ‘I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ He said, ‘You will entice him, and will also prevail. Go out and do so.’
Now therefore, behold, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you.”
Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did Yahweh’s Spirit go from me to speak to you?”
Micaiah said, “Behold, you will see on that day, when you go into an inner room to hide yourself.”
The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king’s son.
Say, ‘Thus says the king, “Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace.”’”
Micaiah said, “If you return at all in peace, Yahweh has not spoken by me.” He said, “Listen, all you people!”
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself, and go into the battle; but you put on your robes.” The king of Israel disguised himself, and went into the battle.
Now the king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two captains of his chariots, saying, “Don’t fight with small nor great, except only with the king of Israel.”
When the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “Surely that is the king of Israel!” and they turned aside to fight against him. Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.

A certain man drew his bow at random, and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, “Turn your hand, and carry me out of the battle; for I am severely wounded.”
The battle increased that day. The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and died at evening. The blood ran out of the wound into the bottom of the chariot.
A cry went throughout the army about the going down of the sun, saying, “Every man to his city, and every man to his country!”
So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria.
They washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood where the prostitutes washed themselves; according to Yahweh’s word which he spoke.
Now the rest of the acts of Ahab, and all that he did, and the ivory house which he built, and all the cities that he built, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
So Ahab slept with his fathers; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.

He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He didn’t turn aside from it, doing that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes. However the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.
Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he fought, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
The remnant of the sodomites, that remained in the days of his father Asa, he put away out of the land.
There was no king in Edom. A deputy ruled.
Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they didn’t go; for the ships wrecked at Ezion Geber.
Then Ahaziah the son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships.” But Jehoshaphat would not.
Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in his father David’s city. Jehoram his son reigned in his place.
Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, in which he made Israel to sin.
He served Baal and worshiped him, and provoked Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger, in all the ways that his father had done so.

footnotes.content: Three years of peace—such a fragile thing. We see a kingdom free from warfare, yet notice how quickly that rest becomes restlessness for a man like Ahab. The heart bent on gold and glory will never be satisfied by safety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoshaphat traveled from Judah to Samaria—south came north to strengthen a bond. Yet in visiting Ahab, this good man was drawn into counsel he should have fled. Proximity to the wicked has a way of clouding judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ramoth Gilead—a real city east of Jordan, a Levitical refuge city lost to Syria. Ahab's question sounds reasonable: why leave what belongs to us in enemy hands? But listen closely: his words betray a heart nursing old wounds, looking for any cause to fight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am as you are, my people as your people." Jehoshaphat bound himself to Ahab with beautiful words—but we know what follows. How often do we promise too quickly, before we listen, before we ask the Lord? Those swift words cost him blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Please inquire first for Yahweh's word." There it is—the one wise voice. Jehoshaphat catches himself mid-rush and asks for the Lord's counsel. Even a man made restless by Ahab's hunger still remembers to ask. This small act of seeking changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four hundred prophets, united in one word: "Go." All speaking peace, all proclaiming victory—yet Jehoshaphat remains uneasy. There is a peculiar danger in a crowd of voices all saying what a king wants to hear. Unity of the crowd is not a mark of truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoshaphat asks the crucial question: isn't there a prophet of Yahweh among all these men? His instinct—honed, perhaps, by years of walking humbly before God—tells him that so much agreement feels hollow. One who truly seeks the Lord knows the difference between comfort and truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I hate him, for he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil." Here is Ahab's confession. A king who hates a prophet hates the Lord—and proves it by wanting good news instead of truth. The measure of a heart is not what it wishes to hear, but what it does with what is true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An officer is sent to fetch Micaiah. Even as the machinery of power moves to summon one man, does anyone suspect he will overturn all four hundred? The Lord often speaks through the lonely and disregarded voice. One man of conviction can shake a kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the gate of Samaria—Samaria was Ahab's capital, northern Israel's seat of power. The kings in their robes, the prophets arrayed before them, all the pageantry of authority. Yet in this moment, a true word is about to pierce through all that show.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah makes horns of iron—a prophet turning to theater, to props, to stir emotion in the crowd. When men who should speak for God resort to spectacle, we are watching the corruption of the office. The Lord's word needs no costume.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the prophets echoed the same word—prosperity, victory, deliverance. Not one of them broke ranks. We see here how conformity becomes a kind of blindness, and how a crowd can reinforce a lie until even its speakers believe it. Truth often stands alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The messenger begs Micaiah: "Please let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak good." Pressure—not from a king, but from his own courier—to buy peace by speaking what the moment demands. How gently temptation wraps itself in reasonableness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As Yahweh lives, what Yahweh says to me, that I will speak." Micaiah's oath, simple and unshakeable. He swears not by the moment's convenience or the crowd's preference, but by the very life of God. Fidelity is costly, but it is always the only option for the faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micaiah speaks first words that mirror the four hundred: "Go up and prosper." A moment of irony—he speaks their language, lets Ahab hear what he wishes, then waits for the king to press for the truth. Sometimes the prophet must show the king his own blindness before speaking the word of judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "How many times do I have to adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in Yahweh's name?" Ahab has asked this before—yet each time, he hates the answer. His demand for truth reveals his real thirst: he wants only the truth that suits him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd." Micaiah paints the true end: not victory, but chaos and grief. The soldiers will die, the kingdom will fall, all because a king refused to turn from his hunger for power. This is what becomes of those who reject the Lord's word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Didn't I tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?" Ahab's complaint to Jehoshaphat reveals his sickness: he sees the prophet's truth as a personal affront. To the hardened heart, faithfulness looks like enmity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him." Now Micaiah takes Ahab beyond earthly battle to the throne of God. What Ahab sees as his moment to seize, God has already seen, already decreed. The heavenly court watches when earthly kings move.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall?" The Lord poses the question—not commanding, but asking. Even in judgment, there is a kind of choice offered. Yet a king bent on his own way needs little enticing; he walks to his own ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "A spirit came out and stood before Yahweh, and said, 'I will entice him.'" Here is the mystery of providence: God permits deception to fall upon those who choose deception. The lying spirit that enters the prophets' mouths is allowed—not commanded, but permitted—to have its way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets." The mechanism of judgment: Ahab's own desire for flattering words becomes the trap. He has chosen to surround himself with those who tell him what he wishes to hear. Now that choice bears its bitter fruit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you." Micaiah speaks it plain: the four hundred are instruments of God's judgment against Ahab. The king's fate is sealed—not by chance, but by the determined will of the Holy One.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah strikes Micaiah on the cheek—the prophet pays in blood for speaking truth. Yet his wound is a kind of seal. Sometimes the mark of the true prophet is not the crowd's applause, but the world's blow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Behold, you will see on that day, when you go into an inner room to hide yourself." Micaiah's reply to Zedekiah is swift—a word of judgment that will prove itself. The time is coming when the prophet's word will be vindicated, when all the flattery will have turned to ash.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micaiah is taken into custody—ordered to be carried to Amon the governor. The sentence precedes the crime: the king is so certain of victory that he already imprisons the prophet who warned him. This is the way of tyrants: they cannot bear a voice they cannot control.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace." Ahab's own words condemn him: he speaks of returning in peace, but Micaiah's word has already decreed otherwise. Pride always speaks most loudly just before the fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If you return at all in peace, Yahweh has not spoken by me." Micaiah stakes his own life on the truth of his word—it is the mark of one who truly bears the Lord's message. No hedging, no safety net. Only faith in the God who sent him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead." They go—despite the warning, despite the truth spoken. This is human choice in all its tragedy: the will to believe what we wish, the rush to grasp what calls to our ambition, even when warned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will disguise myself, and go into the battle; but you put on your robes." Ahab suspects the danger—hence the disguise. Yet no disguise can hide a man from the eyes of the Lord. To strip away our pride and put on truth would save us; to hide in false covering only hastens the judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Syria commanded the captains: seek only the king of Israel. Ramoth Gilead was a place of contest, strategically important on the east bank of the Jordan. This specific military order—to target the king alone—becomes the instrument of his ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captains see Jehoshaphat in his royal robes and turn to attack him. Even Judah's good king, standing at Ahab's side, is drawn into the bloodshed. There is an irony in his preservation: disguised Ahab escapes one blow, while robed Jehoshaphat draws the enemy's blade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captains realize their mistake and break off from chasing Jehoshaphat. For a moment, it seems Ahab's ruse might work—the disguise might save him. Yet no disguise avails against the word of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "A certain man drew his bow at random, and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor." One man, an arrow shot without aim—yet it finds the only exposed place. This is how God's purposes move: through the small, the overlooked, the seemingly random.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and died at evening. The blood ran out of the wound into the bottom of the chariot." Ahab dies propped upright, pretending strength until the last breath—a portrait of pride maintaining its façade even as life drains away. How often do we die to ourselves only in appearance, never in truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "A cry went throughout the army about the going down of the sun." The word spreads with the sunset—the king is dead, all is lost. In one day, the promise of victory has become chaos. The will of God, hidden from human sight, accomplishes itself through events we call chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria." The body is borne home to the capital, to a tomb of honor. Yet all the dignity of burial cannot undo what the king became in his living—a man who refused the Lord's word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood where the prostitutes washed themselves; according to Yahweh's word which he spoke." The word spoken through Elijah is fulfilled—the king's blood is licked by dogs, not honored. This is how the Lord's word measures its fulfillment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler pauses to note all Ahab built—his ivory house, his cities, his works. Yet what use are they now? He has left behind splendor, but taken away nothing. A soul bent on glory finds only dust at the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "So Ahab slept with his fathers; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place." The king goes to his rest, his son rises to the throne, and the patterns that led to ruin will repeat themselves. This is how sin works: one generation passes it to the next like a cursed inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoshaphat began to reign in the fourth year of Ahab. The historian marks the overlap of these kings' reigns—north and south, divided in house yet sometimes bound in alliance. These are the years when faithfulness stands in stark relief against the world's idolatry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years. Jerusalem was his seat, his mother's name was remembered. He had length of days, a throne, a name—yet his greatest victory lay in the choices made in a single day at Ramoth Gilead, when he questioned the prophets and prepared to step back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He didn't turn aside from it, doing that which was right in Yahweh's eyes." Jehoshaphat's continuity—he kept his father's path. Yet even doing right, he stumbled into alliance with the wicked. How vigilant we must be, lest good intentions draw us into partnership with those who serve other gods.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "However the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places." Even Jehoshaphat's faithfulness had limits—the high places remained. A good king may walk righteously and still leave standing the idols that should fall. Partial obedience is obedience half-finished.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel." After the carnage at Ramoth Gilead, peace is made between the two kingdoms. Yet what manner of peace follows a day of blood? The chronicler records it without judgment, yet we see how the living must find their way forward after the righteous word has been spoken and rejected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The remnant of the sodomites, that remained in the days of his father Asa, he put away out of the land." Jehoshaphat's reform—he removes the last traces of the idolatrous remnant. Where his father began the work, he completed it. There is worth in faithfully finishing what a faithful forerunner started.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "There was no king in Edom. A deputy ruled." Edom, the southern neighbor, had no throne, only a regent's hand. This political detail marks the shifting balance—when one kingdom weakens, others rise. The waves of power ebb and flow, yet only the Lord's kingdom stands forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold—Tarshish represents the distant seas, Ophir the sources of wealth. He built for trade and treasure, but the ships wrecked at Ezion Geber. Even a good king's schemes can founder if they are not ordered to the Lord's purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaziah asks to send servants with Jehoshaphat in the ships. The son of Ahab reaches out, perhaps hoping to share in wealth or partnership. Jehoshaphat refuses. Even after bloodshed, even after Ramoth Gilead, he holds a line: his people will not be entangled with the house of Ahab.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in his father David's city. Jehoram his son reigned in his place." The good king rests in the city of David, in the tomb of his lineage. His legacy lies not in gold gathered or ships built, but in a kingdom that walked in the Lord's way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign—another generation of the northern kingdom's kings. His throne rose in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat; his reign would last two years. So brief, so little—and yet enough to choose evil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He did that which was evil in Yahweh's sight, and walked in the way of his father." The son follows the father's path, choosing darkness as his father chose it. The pattern repeats—not because it must, but because the heart that will not turn to the Lord will always turn to its own ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He served Baal and worshiped him, and provoked Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger, in all the ways that his father had done so." Readers today hear an echo in these words: how little has changed. Still, men and women choose the work of their own hands over the face of the Living God. Still, the Lord watches, patient and grieved, as His people turn away. As of 2026-10, we see this same old story unfolding, and we should be humbled by what little progress the human heart has made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
